Unity has been working with an investment bank to evaluate its options following the approach, the people said. No deal is certain, and the plan and terms may still change, they added. Unity declined to comment. Silver Lake and PIF did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A deal would take private one of the largest providers of software tools used to create video games and other real-time 3D applications. It would rank among the biggest leveraged buyouts in the software sector in recent years. SILVER LAKE, PIF TIES TO GAMING Silver Lake and PIF have partnered on major gaming deals before. The EA take-private, which also included Affinity Partners, was among the largest leveraged buyouts ever. Unity’s game engine and developer tools are already used by Scopely, the developer behind “Monopoly Go!,” and Niantic, the creator of “Pokemon Go.” Both are owned by a group that includes PIF, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners. Silver Lake, one of the world’s largest technology-focused private equity firms, has a long-standing relationship with Unity. It invested up to $400 million in the company in 2017 and remains among its largest shareholders. Silver Lake’s Egon Durban also sits on Unity’s board, a dual role that would typically lead him to recuse himself from board deliberations on a sale. Unity on Thursday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street estimates, helped by strong growth in its advertising and game-development businesses. Revenue rose 32 per cent to $622.1 million, and adjusted earnings were 44 cents per share. Strong growth in Unity’s AI-powered Vector advertising platform helped it post its first quarterly profit on a GAAP basis since going public in September 2020. San Francisco-based Unity makes the software engine behind thousands of mobile, console and PC games, and its technology is increasingly used in automotive design, filmmaking, architecture and industrial simulation. Its platform lets developers create and run interactive 3D content across multiple devices and operating systems. Founded in Denmark in 2004, Unity since going public has expanded beyond its core game engine business into advertising technology and broader real-time 3D software.

Zelenskiy says Ukraine must adapt to new US political realities, solve Patriot air defence issue

Reuters

06 November, 2026 04:30 am IST

Nov 5 (Reuters) – Ukraine must adapt to the new realities of US politics to build dialogue and address its needs for more foreign aid and bolstered air defences to counter Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in an interview broadcast on Thursday.

Zelenskiy has made considerable effort to smooth over a volatile relationship with US President Donald Trump, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting during which he was accused of being ungrateful for Washington’s aid.

US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia on resolving the conflict are scheduled to resume next week in Abu Dhabi.

Show Full Article

Zelenskiy, attending an Ibero-American summit in Spain, told Ukrainian television channel TSN that Kyiv had to adapt to a changed US political landscape after voters in US midterm elections put Democrats in control of Congress.

“Ukraine has to move forward towards the new political infrastructure in the United States of America,” he said.

“We have to move quickly. Without doubt, we have to unite the bipartisan support that we get. Understanding the power shifts, we should build up our dialogue the right way. I believe we have the chance to increase support.”

Ukraine needs to become stronger through aid packages and recover what he described as $16 billion in assistance that he said Washington promised but did not deliver.

PATRIOT MISSILES TOP PRIORITY

The country’s main priority, he said, was enhancing air defences as the war against Russia extends past the 4-1/2-year mark. That meant ensuring supplies of missiles for the US Patriot air defence system.

“If we don’t solve the Patriot problem, it will get very tough for us,” he said. “This issue could be solved by Europe, some countries outside Europe and, of course, the United States of America. This is the No. 1 priority.”

The US State Department said last week it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion. The missiles are not expected to be delivered until the early 2030s, however.

Zelenskiy said he was also working to ensure Ukraine has enough operating F-16 fighter jets over the next five to six months.

Ukraine is facing another winter of Russian strikes on its energy sector, with the situation in the capital Kyiv being “the most difficult,” he said.

Zelenskiy said EU, NATO and US officials, meeting this week in Brussels, were working out proposals for security guarantees at the end of the conflict and making some progress. US envoy Jared Kushner, writing on X, called the talks productive and substantive.

(Reporting by Ron Popeski and Bogdan Kochubey; Editing by Rod Nickel)

item.title: Ontario’s Lecce warns that Democrats offer no tariff cure
item.description: Canada shouldn’t expect the United States to lift tariffs simply because Democrats won control of Congress, Ontario Energy and Mines Minister said.
item.dc:creator: Northern Miner Staff
item.content:encoded:
Ontario’s Lecce warns that Democrats offer no tariff cure

Frédéric Tomesco | November 5, 2026 | 4:00 pm Regulatory Issues   Canada   USA   Aluminum   Copper   Nickel

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce (in a file photo) says Canada still faces U.S. protectionism regardless of the midterm elections. Credit: The Northern Miner

Canada shouldn’t expect the United States to lift tariffs simply because Democrats won control of Congress , Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said.

Speaking two days after the U.S. midterm elections, Lecce said the outcome could strengthen Prime Minister Mark Carney’s negotiating position. Still, protectionism runs through both major U.S. political parties, which will leave Canadian exporters exposed even after President Donald Trump leaves office, he cautioned.

“I’m just not convinced it materially changes our fundamental reality on the ground,” Lecce said of the U.S. midterm election results in a lunchtime speech Thursday to the Empire Club of Toronto. “The change of the composition of Congress doesn’t change the policy position of America vis-a-vis tariffs.”

Lecce’s remarks underscore the gap between securing a trade agreement and eliminating tariffs. For Canadian metals producers, a trade deal may offer greater certainty without removing the tariffs that raise the cost of selling into the U.S. market.

Lame-duck Trump

Democrats won both the House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s elections, giving them power to challenge Trump’s agenda when the new Congress convenes in January. The results leave the Republican president facing an opposition-controlled Congress for his final two years in office.

While U.S. political analysts pointed to voter frustration over high prices, the Iran war and government corruption as key factors behind Tuesday’s outcome, Lecce insists trade friction with Canada figured prominently in the campaign.

“Tariffs were on the ballot,” he said. “We stayed in our lane, but it’s clear that Canada was on the ballot.”

New momentum

Negotiations between the neighbours and trading partners have been showing fresh momentum. Carney said Tuesday that Washington had dropped demands affecting Canada’s ability to negotiate agreements with other countries. Trump, meanwhile, said a deal was close, Reuters reported.

Carney’s recent comments on the state of talks are “a good signal,” Lecce said. The Democrats’ win Tuesday “perhaps will enable a better hand for Prime Minister Carney and the national government to land a deal.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford should get credit for pressing Carney to reject an earlier agreement that would have entrenched tariffs, Lecce added.

Recounting a conversation between the two leaders, Lecce said Ford told Carney this summer: “’Do not sign a bad deal that will lock us and create the precedent of acceptance of tariffs in perpetuity. No deal is materially better than a good deal.”

Ford also made it clear to Carney that Ontario would oppose the deal publicly, according to Lecce.

Wider dispute

Ottawa suspended negotiations with the U.S. in August. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on $27.6 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian countermeasures .

The dispute extends beyond those measures. According to Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, U.S. sectoral tariffs on covered steel, aluminum and copper products range from 15% to 50%, subject to product and content rules. Certain other tariffs apply even when Canadian goods qualify for preferential treatment under the continental trade agreement.

The bilateral talks are unfolding alongside negotiations over the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement, or CUSMA. The pact replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement in July 2020, following renegotiation during Trump’s first presidency.

Washington declined to extend CUSMA in its current form at the July 1 review. That triggered annual reviews rather than immediate expiry: the agreement’s existing term runs to 2036, and the three countries can jointly approve another 16-year term.

Canada has explicitly linked those discussions to relief from sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. Preserving CUSMA and resolving the tariff dispute therefore remain connected negotiating objectives.

Diversification

Even as efforts advance to rebuild the American relationship, Canada and Ontario should continue to deepen ties with other nations, Lecce argued.

“We should strengthen that relationship [with the U.S.], get it back on track, but be very vigorous in diversification,” he said. Ontario’s goal is “to make sure we are less exposed, less shocked by that vulnerability when conservatively, well over 75% of our trade is going to one nation.”

Even so, “it doesn’t mean that we can’t hope for some return to what I’d call just normal, respectful civil dialog with the most foundational relationship on earth, which is the United States.”

Nov 5 : TASER maker Axon Enterprise said on Thursday it would invest an additional $1.2 billion in drone maker Skydio and become its exclusive distributor in the US and Canada. The deal highlights growing demand for drones among police, emergency response and government agencies. Here are some more details: • Shares of Axon slumped about 14 per cent to $329 in extended trading after it lowered its annual revenue growth forecast and missed analyst estimates for third-quarter profit

• The investment will increase Axon's stake in Skydio to about 37 per cent, valuing the drone company at $5.2 billion pre-money • Skydio develops AI-powered autonomous drones used by public safety agencies and military customers across the US • It said priority response times at agencies using Axon's Drone as First Responder (DFR) program have been reduced by as much as 65 per cent, with drones arriving before officers on about 80 per cent of deployed calls • The deal consists of a mix of cash and Axon stock, with the transactions expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027 • Additionally, Axon posted an adjusted profit per share of $1.72, missing Wall Street expectations of $1.88 apiece, according to data compiled by LSEG • The company trimmed its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast to about 30 per cent, citing "exclusion of three Federal Dedrone deployments totaling about $130 million"

Analysis:Japanese savers have rediscovered interest rates and banks are feeling it

A man walks past the headquarters of the Bank of Japan in Tokyo, Japan, October 26, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Kyung-Hoon

06 Nov 2026 06:02AM (Updated: 06 Nov 2026 06:21AM)

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 6 : For years, Japanese savers left their cash in bank accounts that paid next to nothing because few things paid much more. With government bonds now yielding four times as much as deposits, that no longer holds and banks are starting to worry. When the Bank of Japan last week declared victory in its near 14-year battle to lift inflation to its 2 per cent target, it closed a long chapter of near-zero interest rates. Now, rising bond yields are making households more sensitive to returns on their money, fuelling a boom in government bond purchases and prompting some to shift a portion of the $7 trillion they hold out of bank deposits. Takashi Kamachi, a 46-year-old self-employed businessman in Osaka, recently moved 600,000 yen ($3,785.01) of his teenage son's gift money, held for years in a Japan Post Bank account, into retail government bonds (JGBs).

"Banks are promoting time deposits again, but I thought government bonds looked far more attractive, perhaps four or five times better in terms of returns," he said. To be sure, the shift is still modest. However, policymakers hope households will eventually play a bigger role in funding Japan's massive budget as stable holders of government debt, and help fill a hole left by the BOJ's diminishing JGB purchases. "Foreign investors can help fill the gap, but what Japan really needs is a stable buyer base, and that means households," said Kenji Nakanishi, a senior ruling party lawmaker and key advocate of expanding retail ownership of government bonds. 'INTEREST RATES EXIST' Retail Japanese government bond sales in the April-October period have nearly doubled from a year earlier to 6 trillion yen. Over last three consecutive months, monthly sales have exceeded 1 trillion yen, as yields on popular retail bonds climbed above 2 per cent, far outstripping bank deposit rates that mostly remain below 1 per cent. "People are starting to realise that interest rates exist," said Takayuki Nakagawa, general manager of retail marketing at SBI Securities, Japan's largest seller of retail government bonds. Many buyers are first-time investors seeking a safe alternative to bank deposits, according to Nakagawa. Drawn by a government guarantee of principal, they represent the same conservative savers banks have traditionally relied on for funding, he said. Despite the BOJ lifting its policy rates, commercial banks have kept deposit rates low to minimise funding costs, offering around 0.5 per cent on one-year deposits, not enough to beat inflation. In contrast, 3- and 5-year retail notes and 10-year floaters all offer coupons above 2 per cent. Japanese households hold roughly 2.50 quadrillion yen in financial assets, according to BOJ data, with cash and deposits accounting for about 1.13 quadrillion yen. Even with that demand, household holdings of government bonds account for less than 1 per cent of their financial assets, compared with roughly 2 per cent for US households' holdings of Treasury securities. JGBs must also compete with global and domestic equities, which have already attracted a steady stream of funds from younger investors seeking higher returns. Eager to find sources of revenue to fund their spending, some lawmakers want to make JGBs more attractive, such as through longer-duration products and incentives such as inheritance-tax benefits. "Now that momentum is finally building, this is exactly the time to give it an extra push," Nakanishi said. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama wants to improve the appeal of retail government bonds. Her ministry, for one, is studying the launch of additional retail bond products, it said on Thursday, while also calling for discussions on preferential tax treatment for buyers. PUSHBACK The idea, however, faces pushback from some lawmakers who fret it would widen income disparity by benefiting already wealthy households. Meanwhile, commercial banks fear a shift into bonds could drain deposits, leaving less ammunition to profit from increasing borrowing demand. Some bank officials say they are already seeing once loyal customers shift money into JGBs. "Preferential treatment for retail government bonds would be a problem," said a senior regional bank official, who requested anonymity. Bank lending has consistently outpaced deposit growth this year, with loans rising 5-6 per cent from a year earlier while deposits grew only around 2 per cent, according to BOJ data, forcing lenders to compete more aggressively for household savings. "A rapid and excessive shift of funds from bank deposits into retail government bonds could weaken the credit-creation function banks are responsible for and affect their ability to supply growth capital to the economy," Mizuho Bank head Masahiko Kato, who is also chair of a banking lobby, said in September. There are also questions about financing Japan's huge debt with household savings. Foreign investors have increased their presence in the JGB market, raising concerns that yields could become more vulnerable to sharp swings in global sentiment. The BOJ's share of the JGB and T-bill market has fallen to 41.2 per cent in June 2026 from a peak of 47.9 per cent in December 2023, as it tapered bond purchases to unwind monetary stimulus. Banks' share has more than halved to 17.8 per cent since 2013, when the BOJ deployed a huge asset-buying scheme. Takero Doi, a professor at Keio University, said instead of boosting retail bond demand, policymakers should focus on reducing government debt. "You could simply end up seeing households replacing banks as buyers of retail government bonds," he said. "That won't solve the underlying problem." ($1 = 158.5200 yen)

(Additional reporting by Takaya Yamaguchi, Noriyuki Hirata, Takahiko Wada and Miho Uranaka; Editing by Sam Holmes)

Source: Reuters

Two Egyptian army officers killed in gold-mining crackdown on southern border, military says

CAIRO, Nov 5 (Reuters) – Two Egyptian army officers, including a high-ranking border guard officer, were killed during a military crackdown on illegal gold mining along Egypt’s southern border with Sudan, a military spokesperson said on Thursday.

The military launched the campaign to counter illegal gold mining in the Eastern Desert in June, with the first three phases complete.  The military said the fourth phase was due to begin on Saturday, adding the campaign intended to strengthen state control over Egyptian territory and protect national resources.

It was not immediately clear when the two officers were killed, and the spokesperson did not specify the timing of their deaths.

Show Full Article

The military spokesperson said authorities had detained 151 Egyptians and 540 foreigners during the campaign.

The campaign has drawn attention after the rights monitor Emergency Lawyers said in October that at least 72 artisanal miners had been killed in an airstrike in northern Sudan, close to the Egyptian border. The group blamed the Egyptian Air Force for the strike.

Egypt’s military did not refer to the reported strike or the deaths at the time. In a statement then, it said a phase of its campaign against illegal gold mining in southern Egypt was under way after it dropped warning leaflets on what it described as “criminal elements.”

Artisanal gold mining has risen in northern Sudan since Sudan’s civil war disrupted livelihoods. Gold has become a key revenue source during the conflict, while experts and industry participants say much of it is smuggled into Egypt through a porous and disputed border area that includes the mineral-rich Halayeb and Shalateen regions.

The Egyptian military spokesperson said there was coordination with Sudan, including recent meetings between Egyptian and Sudanese officials. He said the armed forces of both countries exchanged information on securing the Egypt-Sudan border.

(Reporting by Ali Khafagi, Nayera Abdallah, Hatem Maher, Enas Alashray and Yomna Ehab; Writing by Enas Alashray; Editing by Chris Reese and Rod Nickel)

item.title: Bank of Canada keeps 2% inflation target in mandate renewal
item.description: The Bank of Canada and federal government have agreed to keep a target of two per cent inflation at the core of the central bank’s mandate.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada and federal government have agreed to keep a target of two per cent inflation at the core of the central bank’s mandate. The Bank of Canada sets its benchmark interest rate independently from the federal government but it gets its inflation-targetting mandate from Ottawa. The Bank of Canada said in a release announcing the renewal of its five-year mandate today that its inflation target has served Canadians well in recent decades. The central bank will continue to set monetary policy to make sure annual inflation dips neither too far below or above two per cent, but it retains flexibility to respond to economic shocks. The Bank of Canada increased its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years last week as monetary policymakers fear inflationary pressures could start to spread. The bank announced the mandate renewal minutes after the federal Liberals outlined its economic projections and fiscal track in Budget 2026 on Thursday. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Commentary: Who keeps crashing China’s stock market?

Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion.

An investor walks past an electronic screen showing stock information at a brokerage house in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, January 21, 2015. REUTERS/China Daily

Shuli Ren

FAST

HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue.  Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance – informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell. In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48 per cent. THE BLAME GAME So who’s been selling? The blame game has already begun.

FILE PHOTO: People walk past the headquarters of the People's Bank of China (PBOC), the central bank, in Beijing, China September 28, 2018. REUTERS/Jason Lee/File Photo

Shiva Capital Group, one of China’s biggest hedge funds, has pointed the finger at insurers. In a recent letter to clients, founder Hong Liang accused the insurance firms of piling into technology stocks near their July peak, only to slash positions in late September. The behaviour was “truly baffling”, lamented the prominent investor, who has a large following on the mainland. Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time. China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the United States, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound.  NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness.  That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

Related:

Commentary: Beijing cracks down on cross-border investment but it is up to something grander

Commentary: What China’s underperforming tech stocks say about its real economy

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance, for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2 per cent of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9 per cent in 2025.  Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market – a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.  In recent days, authorities have issued window guidance to several major insurers, requiring them to report their equity holdings, refrain from cutting their losses, and align investment decisions with broader economic goals. WHO WILL BE LEFT TO BLAME? The government now appears to be grappling with an unintended consequence of its own policy.  Insurers may be more patient investors than hedge funds, but they still have to manage risk and meet claims and other liabilities. That limits their ability to sit indefinitely on mounting losses – and can force them to cut exposure during severe market downturns.  Insurers, in other words, cannot be as reliably countercyclical as the “national team”, whose primary purpose is market stabilisation.

Related:

Commentary: China is betting on spreading AI faster than the US can contain it

Commentary: This bad movie is a good guide to China’s stock market

On its latest earnings call, executives at China Pacific Insurance Group acknowledged that equity investing had become “complicated” and that portfolios needed to be managed so market volatility didn’t damage short-term returns. In the third quarter, profits at China’s five major listed insurers plunged, largely because of the decline in domestic stocks. The experience points to an uncomfortable reality: For insurers, reliable dividend payers such as Bank of Jiangsu may ultimately be better suited to their liabilities than capital-intensive chipmakers. Few in China – including Shiva’s Liang – are willing to say publicly that policy missteps themselves may be contributing to poor stock market performance. Instead, blame has fallen on everything from thin liquidity to indiscriminate selling. But that raises a bigger question: Why does China keep suffering stock market routs? Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts – in 2018, 2024 and now. The next time the PBOC has to put out a fire, who will be left to blame? Foreigners, hedge funds and now even state-owned insurers have all had their turn.

Source: Bloomberg/ch

AI data center firm IREN delays Microsoft AI deliveries, plans $15 billion spending push

FILE PHOTO: The words "AI Artificial Intelligence" and a keyboard in this illustration taken October 19, 2026. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo

FAST

Nov 5 : AI data center firm IREN on Thursday delayed some infrastructure deliveries for Microsoft and laid out another $15 billion in spending, even as a rout in AI stocks puts the sector's massive buildout under pressure. Australia-based IREN also beat quarterly revenue estimates on strong growth in its AI cloud business, lifting its shares 4 per cent in extended trading. The stock closed down about 17 per cent during a broader selloff that hit chipmakers and so-called neocloud companies, including IREN rival CoreWeave, particularly hard as Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterms fanned fears of tougher regulation of the technology. IREN said the delay to infrastructure being built for Microsoft would not result in financial penalties as it stemmed from the software giant requesting network-design changes. However, the company pushed the timeline for making operational its more than $4 billion annualized run-rate revenue target to January from year-end, and said the timing could extend to the end of February. The company said the shift followed a customer-requested design change and supplier timing.

The Windows maker is tightening oversight of some data center projects run by neocloud providers including IREN, Nebius and Nscale amid delays and rising costs, Bloomberg News reported earlier on Thursday. Microsoft is stepping away from projects it considers risky and weighing whether to sign new deals with such providers as it focuses more heavily on expanding its own data centers, according to the report. IREN, valued at some $7 billion, is building 200 megawatts of data-center capacity for Microsoft in Texas. The company said it would keep investing significantly in computing equipment and infrastructure as it expands its AI cloud business, estimating about $15 billion in capital expenditure over the rest of its fiscal year. Its quarterly filing showed capital commitments of $18.95 billion at the end of September, up from $13.81 billion three months earlier, while GPU hardware on its balance sheet nearly tripled to $5.82 billion from $2.04 billion. Construction in progress stood at about $4.61 billion. IREN's AI cloud revenue in the first quarter rose to $200 million from $71 million in the prior three months. Total revenue rose to $228 million in the quarter ended September 30, compared with analysts' average estimate of $221.28 million, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company said its assets and revenue were supported by contracts with Nvidia, Microsoft and 13 others, with roughly two-thirds of its revenue backlog tied to investment-grade counterparties. IREN executives said on a post-earnings call that the company exited September with $1 billion in annualized run-rate revenue and expects roughly one-quarter of that amount to be recognized in the December quarter.

Source: Reuters

item.title: Auto dealers warn high inventories, financing costs may hit demand
item.description: Passenger vehicle inventory stood at 43-45 days despite record wholesale dispatches, FADA said, while expressing hope that strong festive-season retail sales would help reduce stock levels ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Auto / Auto dealers warn high inventories, financing costs may hit demand

Auto dealers warn high inventories, financing costs may hit demand Passenger vehicle inventory stood at 43-45 days despite record wholesale dispatches, FADA said, while expressing hope that strong festive-season retail sales would help reduce stock levels

Passenger vehicle inventory remained at about 43-45 days despite record wholesale dispatches

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:57 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Indian auto dealers warned on Friday that high inventories, rising financing costs and signs of rural stress could threaten post-festive demand despite record industry sales, with November retail sales key to clearing excess stock.   While automakers have reported strong wholesale sales, dealers say the focus is shifting to whether retail demand can sustain growth beyond the festive season.   Fada said October retail sales were hit by a delayed festive calendar, with passenger vehicle registrations falling 14 per cent from a year earlier and two-wheeler sales declining 28 per cent.   "The inventory today is not a major concern, but if it remains at these levels by the end of December, it becomes a major concern because dealers start losing money," Sai Giridhar, president of Fada, told Reuters.     Passenger vehicle inventory remained at 43-45 days in October, above the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations' recommended 21-day level. Also Read

Giridhar said dealers were already seeing demand soften in some rural pockets affected by deficient rainfall, particularly in the two-wheeler segment, though he expects purchases delayed by the later festive season to support November sales.   Moreover, about 31 per cent of dealers reported a moderate or material impact from higher financing costs and loan repayments, while repeated vehicle price increases had eroded much of the benefit from last year's tax cuts, Fada said.   "If inventory continues at around 45 days, it will put pressure on dealers and OEMs to give extra discounts and liquidate inventory," Giridhar said.   Fada's comments follow robust October wholesales, including a record monthly sales figures for industry leader Maruti Suzuki, though analysts said part of the growth reflected inventory build-up at dealerships ahead of the festive season.

item.title: Wisconsin Baby Dies of Measles in First State Death in 36 Years
item.description: Wisconsin reported its first measles death in more than three decades on Thursday, the latest state to suffer a fatality from a virus that was long eradicated in the US but recently surged back amid a wave of anti-vaccine sentiment.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Wisconsin reported its first measles death in more than three decades on Thursday, the latest state to suffer a fatality from a virus that was long eradicated in the US but recently surged back amid a wave of anti-vaccine sentiment.The death occurred in an infant, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said in a statement. It is the third US measles death within the last week — matching the number of deaths in all of 2025. In the preceding 25 years, the US typically had no deaths.Across the US, measles has been spreading at an increasing rate as vaccination uptake has declined. That’s eroded the herd immunity that protects people who cannot be vaccinated like infants and the immunocompromised. At least 45 states have reported infections for a total of 4,852 people, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The highly contagious virus has been spreading in the southwestern part of Wisconsin and nine people have been hospitalized in connection with the outbreak, according to the health department.“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Wisconsin State Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. With the US measles case count at its highest in decades, its long-held status as a measles eliminated country is under threat. An outside group of experts is scheduled to meet next week and review the data to determine whether the US has seen continued transmission of the disease for more than 12 months. This week, Pennsylvania confirmed a sixth death from measles and New York reported its first. Utah, South Carolina and Texas have also seen particularly bad flareups of measles over the last year.Wisconsin said local healthcare providers and public health staff have delivered more than 42,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine since August. No vaccine is perfect, but the MMR is 97% effective after two doses. One to three people out of 1,000 are likely to die from measles, according to the CDC. The respiratory infection can cause flu-like symptoms and a distinct red rash across the body. Complications include brain swelling, pneumonia and death. The CDC has confirmed only four of the deaths this year. After Pennsylvania reported its first fatalities, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested the state’s governor Josh Shapiro may have fabricated them for political gain — sparking a verbal dispute. The CDC is working on a national measles death definition with an outside group of epidemiologists.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Texas Governor-elect Hinojosa plans to protect citizens from data centres, warns Musk to submit to 'their terms'
item.description: Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has highlighted her plans to bring in “laws to protect Texans” from data centres, which she said were taking advantage of rural communities in the state.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Governor-elect Hinojosa plans to protect citizens from data centres, warns Musk to submit to 'their terms' Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has highlighted her plans to bring in “laws to protect Texans” from data centres, which she said were taking advantage of rural communities in the state. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 09:53 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 09:53 IST

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (L) and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk (R) (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has highlighted her plans to bring in “laws to protect Texans” from data centres, which she said were taking advantage of rural communities in the state. Speaking to CNN, Hinojosa stated, “Right now, what has happened is data centres have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.” She maintained that Texas has been a pro-business state; however, she aims at business partnerships that benefit Texans. "We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans,” she told CNN. "So the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we’re doing with data centres until we have those protections. We can have a strong economy, strong industry and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I’ll make sure, as governor, I lead to ensure that happens," she added. While she did not rule out building of data centres in Texas, she discussed the communities having a stake in decision-making. She said, "It is not that I hate data centres. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas. And that stops when I’m governor.” When asked whether SpaceX CEO Elon Musk might move out of Texas, Gina Hinojosa said, "We can have a strong working relationship with Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas." When asked about blocking the sale of a Texas state park to SpaceX, and whether Musk might leave the state over itm the Governor-elect said, “We have to have balance. These are our beaches we’re talking about. I mean, selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable. It’s unacceptable. Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas Constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas because they are our beaches." Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor's race, defeating Republican Governor Greg Abbott. Hinojosa ended more than three decades of Republican domination in the office as the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990 and the state's first Latina governor. (ANI)

item.title: Australia ropes in Michael Hussey as coaching consultant for 2027 Ashes, ODI World Cup, 2028 Olympics
item.description: Australia have appointed former batter Michael Hussey as a coaching consultant for the 2027 Ashes and ODI World Cup, while also assigning him the role of T20 advisor for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics ...
item.content:encoded:
Australia ropes in Michael Hussey as coaching consultant for 2027 Ashes, ODI World Cup, 2028 Olympics Australia have appointed former batter Michael Hussey as a coaching consultant for the 2027 Ashes and ODI World Cup, while also assigning him the role of T20 advisor for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and the T20 World Cup, which will be jointly hosted by Australia and New Zealand ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 09:52 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 09:52 IST

Michael Hussey. (Photo/Reuters) . Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Australia have appointed former batter Michael Hussey as a coaching consultant for the 2027 Ashes and ODI World Cup, while also assigning him the role of T20 advisor for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and the T20 World Cup, which will be jointly hosted by Australia and New Zealand. Hussey has undertaken short-term assignments with the Australian team under head coach Andrew McDonald in recent years, primarily serving as an additional batting consultant ahead of the annual Perth Test, as per Cricinfo. However, his involvement has been limited by his commentary commitments and coaching roles with Chennai Super Kings in the IPL and Welsh Fire in The Hundred. Hussey was also approached to join long-time colleague Stephen Fleming's coaching setup after the New Zealander took charge of England's Test team earlier this year. However, he turned down the opportunity in favour of a more substantial consultancy role with Australia. His new assignment will begin with Australia's upcoming T20I series against England, before he assists the team in its preparations for the New Zealand Test series in Perth. "I am extremely excited about being a part of the team in a more formal and meaningful role in the coming years," Hussey said. "This team has achieved so much in recent times, to which I hope I can add value to the coaching and playing groups ahead of what will be an exciting and challenging period," he added. "Mike has been a highly valued part of our staff in the past and brings a considerable skill set which is complementary to the coaches and players. Not only is his expertise as a player and coach across multiple formats, competitions, and countries invaluable, but so are his qualities as a person," Australia head coach Andrew McDonald said. (ANI)

item.title: "Would rather not destroy rest of the country": Trump's Iran war tone changes after midterm drubbing
item.description: US President Donald Trump stated he would rather not destroy what remains of Iran but may have to, adopting a hesitant tone following the Republicans' midterm defeat. He noted that a final decision on ...
item.content:encoded:
"Would rather not destroy rest of the country": Trump's Iran war tone changes after midterm drubbing US President Donald Trump stated he would rather not destroy what remains of Iran but may have to, adopting a hesitant tone following the Republicans' midterm defeat. He noted that a final decision on the war is approaching soon. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 09:49 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 09:49 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would rather not destroy what remains of Iran but acknowledged that he may have to, adopting a more hesitant line than his previous threats against Tehran following his Republican Party's setback in the US midterm elections. Addressing reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday (local time), Trump noted that a final decision on whether the war was close to escalating was imminent. "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I'll have to," he stated, adding, "You'll know soon enough." He described the ultimate choice in terms of permanence. "We'll make a decision, do we want to go further and just certify it by certifying it, meaning where it'll never happen again?" Trump remarked, estimating that rebuilding the nation would require a quarter of a century. "I think it'll take them 25 years to rebuild the country." This language contrasts with his earlier posture, during which he warned that American forces had yet to begin "destroying what's left" of Iran, keeping additional energy infrastructure and bridges as targets. Previously, during another phase of the conflict, he maintained that reaching a deal was only possible if the United States blew up the remainder of the nation and its leadership. These remarks follow a specific pledge delivered on October 8, when Trump stated that talks with Iran were productive and explicitly ruled out military action before the national ballot. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," he noted at the time, while American media outlets reported that indirect negotiations were ongoing. That commitment has since expired following the conclusion of the vote. Earlier reports had already suggested his hesitation to completely eliminate Iran's remaining military capacity due to the extensive duration required for national reconstruction. Domestically, the ongoing war has created political friction for the administration, keeping fuel costs elevated and contributing to a decline in public approval ratings as the election approached. Whether the administration pursues further military strikes or a negotiated settlement will ultimately dictate the trajectory of a conflict that has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and deeply unsettled energy markets. (ANI)

item.title: "No negotiations till US fulfils seven conditions": Iran security chief says Russia condemned US-Israel strikes
item.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has condemned the US and Israeli strikes against Iran and its nuclear facilities, Iran's security chief, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said as Russia offered support to ...
item.content:encoded:
"No negotiations till US fulfils seven conditions": Iran security chief says Russia condemned US-Israel strikes Russian President Vladimir Putin has condemned the US and Israeli strikes against Iran and its nuclear facilities, Iran's security chief, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said as Russia offered support to end the ongoing war in West Asia, as per IRNA. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 09:48 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 09:48 IST

Russian President Vladimir Putin meets Iranian security council chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Russia

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Russian President Vladimir Putin has condemned the US and Israeli strikes against Iran and its nuclear facilities, Iran's security chief, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said as Russia offered support to end the ongoing war in West Asia, as per IRNA. Rezaei met Putin at the Kremlin Palace on Thursday and delivered a message from Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei. Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Rezaei said that there will be no negotiations with the United States regarding the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, untill Iran's seven conditions are met. Rezaei said, "Russian President Vladimir Putin had forcefully condemned the US and Israel's military aggression against Iran, including the strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities." "Until the Americans fulfil our seven conditions, neither will the Strait of Hormuz be opened, nor will there be any negotiations," he added. Iranian broadcaster Press TV also reported, citing a source, that Rezaei had stated that Tehran does not consider the diplomatic process to be worthwhile until all of the seven conditions are simultaneously implemented. During the meeting, the Russian President stated that Moscow is ready to make every possible effort to bring the ongoing US-Iran war to an end. "Mr Putin said he will do everything he can to help bring the war to an end," Rezaei said, according to Press TV. The two sides also discussed energy cooperation, particularly the construction of gas pipelines connecting Russia and Iran. "We discussed the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran, which would allow Iran to address its domestic gas shortages while also selling Russian gas to neighbouring countries," Rezaei said. The meeting between Putin and Rezaei came amid the United States weighing in on resuming military strikes against Iran after Democrats swept the US Midterm elections. Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held telephone conversations with his counterparts from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Oman amid diplomatic efforts in the region. (ANI)

item.title: AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit
item.description: The investment comes as the gold miner aims to incrementally increase production by the end of the decade.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit

Marina Meireles | November 5, 2026 | 9:55 am Top Companies   Africa   Latin America   Gold

Geita open pit mine, located in northwestern Tanzania, is AngloGold’s largest single gold mining operation. ( Image: AngloGold Ashanti )

AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) plans to invest up to $900 million in expanding brownfield operations across its portfolio, targeting a production increase of 300,000 ounces to 450,000 ounces by 2030.

The investments will focus on the Geita gold mine in Tanzania, Siguiri in Guinea and Cuiabá in Brazil, as well as the ongoing ramp-up at Obuasi in Ghana. The company expects the projects to generate real internal rates of return exceeding 35%, Reuters reported.

“These are high-return, capital efficient projects at our operating mines that are expected to provide high-margin ounces and unlock further value from our portfolio,” AngloGold Ashanti CEO Alberto Calderon said in a statement.

The plan is to use existing infrastructure and operational footprints to reduce risk and optimize capital intensity.

Geita will receive the larger portion of the funding, up to $580 million to raise output to 600,000 ounces by 2030. Cuiabá’s expansion will cost between $200 million and $250 million, adding about 75,000 ounces to its output.

Another $70 million will be put towards the Suguiri mine, looking to add another 100,000 ounces to its production.

Shares in AngloGold Ashanti were up 0.35% to $88.22 apiece by mid-day Thursday in New York, valuing the company at $44.6 billion.

Profit on the rise

AngloGold reported a 12% increase for its EBITDA for Q3 2026 to $1,568 million, from $1,400 million for Q3 2025.

The company said on its Q3 earnings release that the growth is supported by the increase in the average gold price received per ounce to $4,239/oz, from $3,490/oz in the same period in 2025.

AngloGold Ashanti said its full year gold production guidance of 2,800,000 ounces to 3,170,000 ounces is reaffirmed.

Its gold production was about 3.65% more costly than the previous quarter, at $1,534 per ounce due gold royalties and higher fuel costs.

The company also reported that a worker died due to a rockfall at the Sukari underground mine in August 2026. Operations were suspended while investigations took place, but have since resumed.

(With files from Reuters)

Renewed refinery attacks deplete Russian diesel supply as US deal in focus

The attacks mark the end of a temporary pause in strikes, with Russia’s Ryazan and Yaroslavl oil refineries reportedly targeted this week.

A satellite image shows an overview of oil refinery in Ryazan, Russia, on Jul 28, 2024. (Photo: Reuters/Maxar Technologies)

FAST

LONDON: Ukraine's renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries add to Moscow's difficulty in addressing domestic fuel shortages while it ships diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump. The Ryazan oil refinery , one of R us sia's largest, appeared to have come under attack as part of a large drone strike overnight on ind us trial sites in the city, southeast of Moscow, according to a Reuters video analysis. If confirmed, it would be the second refinery to be hit this week following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant, northeast of Moscow, overnight on Monday (Nov 2), marking the breakdown of a pa us e in strikes. Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries this year forced large amounts of processing capacity in western R us sia offline, ca us ing fuel shortages that meant Moscow had to enforce fuel export bans from April onwards.

A ban on diesel exports has been lifted in part and the US struck the deal in October with the Kremlin to resume diesel exports to international markets when Trump was seeking to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on Nov 3, which Trump's Republican Party lost . The city of Ryazan had restored power supply earlier on Thursday as fires at the unnamed ind us trial sites were either contained or put out, the local governor said on social media.

US -R US SIA DIESEL CARGOES ARE IN FOC US At least six Russian diesel cargoes have broadcast that they plan transatlantic voyages, shipping data from Kpler and LSEG show, while two cargoes appeared to have changed course after being previo us ly bound for the US Atlantic coast. No Russian diesel cargo has arrived in the US since the deal , the data show. The first observed US -bound Russian shipment is expected to arrive in New York this weekend, but regulatory, legislative and sanctions concerns mean that its discharge is not guaranteed, Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. "These are commercial loadings, so naturally the details cannot be made public. All the diesel will find its buyers," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call. Tankers often broadcast messages known as signals, such as "Atlantic coast for orders", indicating they are heading for the US Atlantic coast but have no confirmed discharge port, so the crew is awaiting instructions. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russian diesel cargoes destined for the US are continuing on course, in a post on X. There is no connection between diesel tankers changing course and the result of the US midterm elections, Peskov added.

item.title: RBI proposes ₹100 crore limit on bank loans for agri infrastructure
item.description: The RBI has proposed a ₹100 crore aggregate loan limit per borrower for agricultural infrastructure under revised priority sector lending norms.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Banking / RBI proposes ₹100 crore limit on bank loans for agri infrastructure

RBI proposes ₹100 crore limit on bank loans for agri infrastructure The RBI has proposed a ₹100 crore aggregate loan limit per borrower for agricultural infrastructure under revised priority sector lending norms.

The Reserve Bank of India has proposed revised priority sector lending norms, including a ₹100 crore aggregate loan limit per borrower for agricultural infrastructure and higher eligibility limits for education and renewable energy loans. (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India Mumbai 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:16 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The Reserve Bank on Thursday proposed that loans for agricultural infrastructure will be subject to an aggregate sanctioned limit of Rs 100 crore per borrower from the banking system. As part of the ongoing effort towards consolidation of various instructions, the Reserve Bank of India said it has undertaken a review of the extant guidelines relating to Priority Sector Lending (PSL) and proposes to issue directions on the subject for different regulated entities, including commercial banks and regional rural banks. A draft direction on commercial banks proposed an aggregate loan limit of Rs 4 crore per borrowing entity for crop loans, medium and long-term loans for agriculture and allied activities, as well as loans for pre- and post-harvest activities.   It also said: "Loans for agriculture infrastructure will be subject to an aggregate sanctioned limit of Rs 100 crore per borrower from the banking system."   The lending to the agriculture sector will include farm credit (agriculture and allied activities), lending for agriculture infrastructure and ancillary activities. The draft further said that loans to individuals for educational purposes, including vocational courses, not exceeding Rs 25 lakh, will be considered as eligible for priority sector classification. Also Read

RBI tightens cyber oversight of non-bank payment system operators

RBI forms panel for consultation on financial markets, emerging risks

RBI forms financial markets consultative panel headed by Dy Guv Rohit Jain

RBI forms markets panel with Citi, Morgan Stanley, SBI as members

Regarding renewable energy, it said bank loans up to a limit of Rs 35 crore to borrowers for renewable energy-based power generators and for renewable energy-based public utilities -- street lighting systems, remote village electrification -- will be eligible for priority sector classification. For individual households, the loan limit will be Rs 10 lakh per borrower, the draft said. Agriculture, MSMEs, exports, education, housing, social infrastructure, and renewable energy are among the categories under the priority sector. The RBI has also issued separate draft directions for small finance banks, local area banks, and regional rural banks. RBI has invited comments and feedback on the drafts by November 26.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: New wave of bomb hoaxes hits at least 27 passenger flights across Europe
item.description: While no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks".
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

World

New wave of bomb hoaxes hits at least 27 passenger flights across Europe

While no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks".

An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Gonzalo Fuentes)

05 Nov 2026 05:31PM (Updated: 06 Nov 2026 07:12AM)

FAST

PARIS: Hoax bomb threat s disrupted at least 27 passenger flights across Europe on Thursday (Nov 5), forcing unplanned landings by some planes and prompting fighter jets to escort or intercept others, in the second such wave this week. No country has attributed blame for the threat s, which come as many European officials are accusing Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks" , often cheap, easily deniable and not expected to trigger an armed response. At least seven flights and a cruise ship also received hoax threat s on Tuesday. Denmark, Poland and Romania, all affected by Thursday's disruptions, have previously accused Moscow directly of being behind hybrid attacks, while Germany blamed Russia for an August attack on Leipzig airport. Britain , which has in the past blamed Russia, linked Iran to a suspected plot against a US air base. Both Russia and Iran deny any involvement. Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, said most of the countries affected supported Ukraine in its war against Russia's invasion. While analysts at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said a link to Russia's hybrid campaign in Europe was a "realistic probability", they also cautioned that other explanations, including individuals acting on personal grievances and copycat incidents, were also possible. An airport source in Italy told Reuters that an email with the subject line " Threat report" had been sent to several addresses for airlines, airport operators and airport service providers at Rome's Fiumicino and Milan's Malpensa airports. The email, which claimed it was from "fighters of the Male State", said devices had been placed on inbound flights from Helsinki and Dublin and they would explode in 60 minutes. Reuters could not independently confirm who had sent the email and there was no immediate indication of who was behind the other threat s across Europe.

FROM MILAN TO PRAGUE AND BEYOND Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome landed safely at Evreux airport, 100km west of Paris, after being diverted as a security precaution, the Irish airline said in a statement. Quoting the office of French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, Reuters reported that the Airbus A320 plane was diverted to France's Evreux airbase. The situation is being monitored by the Prime Minister's office, it added. According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, an Aer Lingus aircraft turned near Paris and was circling over the Evreux area after declaring an in-flight emergency. France's air force said it had dispatched planes "as soon as the threat was reported", AFP reported.  "The aircraft has been diverted and is being escorted to the Evreux airfield" west of Paris, it added.

An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat, France on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Gonzalo Fuentes)

A Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by charter airline Jettime, on Thursday landed as normal in Vienna after receiving a bomb threat , a spokesperson for the Finnish carrier said. Finnair earlier said that another Finnair flight to Rome had landed after receiving a bomb threat, Reuters reported. According to AFP, t he Helsinki-Rome flight was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts. Reuters, citing a source, reported that a flight operated by Polish airline LOT flying from Warsaw landed safely at Brussels Airport following a suspicious report. A spokesperson for the airport told Belgian media that no additional security measures were necessary. The airport did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

A view of Fiumicino Airport, after a Finnair plane from Helsinki was safely escorted to its scheduled landing in Rome by Italian air force jets following bomb threats that forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe, in Fiumicino, near Rome, Italy on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Remo Casilli)

Bulgarian officials meanwhile reported three aircraft making emergency landings in the Balkan country because of bomb threats. Airplanes flying from Copenhagen and Madrid landed safely in Sofia, the interior minister said, according to broadcaster bTV. A third aircraft, from London, was diverted and landed in Plovdiv, Bulgaria's second-largest city, local media said. The government did not respond to requests for comment. Spanish authorities said that three flights were affected by hoax bomb threats at Madrid's airport on Thursday morning, though they stressed that security forces had ruled out any risk. It is unclear if this includes the plane from Madrid that had landed in Sofia.  Meanwhile, Czech police on Thursday said four planes headed to Prague received bomb threats and the authorities were preparing for their landing, adding they assessed the credibility of the threat s as low. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the threat , which is why all necessary security measures have been activated with minimal impact on passengers and airport operations," the police said on X.  "After landing, all aircraft will undergo pyrotechnic inspections."    CTK News agency later reported that no explosives were found in the four planes that landed in Prague, citing a police spokesperson.  Separately, t he Romanian intelligence agency said on Thursday that a bomb threat was made on a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest, adding the plane landed safely in the Romanian capital, Reuters reported.  Italy's ANSA news agency meanwhile reported on bomb alerts on two flights bound for Milan's Malpensa Airport, both of which have since landed safely.

A screengrab from a video shows a police officer and a sniffer dog inspecting a Ryanair airplane and its baggage, according to Guardia Civil, in Murcia, Spain, Nov 3, 2026. (Image: Reuters/Forta)

The string of incidents comes after about 10 European flights were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday , forcing the brief closure of a Warsaw airport and the scrambling of air force planes in Rome, according to authorities. No explosives were found in the earlier incidents, despite extensive searches on the ground after the planes all took off and landed safely in different European cities just several hours apart, AFP reported.  Irish budget carrier Ryanair appeared to be the worst hit, with four of its flights to different destinations being targeted. Two bomb warnings targeted planes heading to the Polish capital Warsaw, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and one from Heathrow operated by Polish airline LOT, Polish airport authorities said. This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of cheap, deniable disruption efforts. Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation, told Reuters the repeated threats could serve both to disrupt operations and to observe how airlines, airports and national authorities respond. "These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe," Almog said. "Different essential services are experiencing disruption that carries economic costs and can undermine public confidence."

Source: Agencies/lk/fs

item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Coal gasification can save ₹1.5 trillion in forex in 5-7 years: Coal secy

Coal gasification can save ₹1.5 trillion in forex in 5-7 years: Coal secy The Centre has committed financial incentives of ₹46,000 crore under two schemes to encourage coal gasification projects, said Coal Ministry Secretary Vikram Dev Dutt

Coal gasification projects require substantial upfront capital investment as well as support at the state level in terms of electricity, water supply and taxation | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India Panaji 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 2:26 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Coal gasification projects have the potential to save India around ₹1.5 trillion in foreign exchange over the next five to seven years through import substitution, Coal Ministry Secretary Vikram Dev Dutt said on Thursday. The Centre has committed financial incentives of ₹46,000 crore under two schemes to encourage coal gasification projects, Dutt said, addressing the 4th Conference of Mining Ministers on Reforms in the Mines and Coal Sector in South Goa. "Mining with a conscience" should be the guiding principle for responsible miners, the official added. He said coal gasification, which converts coal into synthetic gas (syngas), can help manufacture several products that India currently imports in substantial quantities.   "If the coal gasification projects get underway and gain scale, we would be succeeding in about five to seven years in saving about Rs one and a half trillion potentially of foreign exchange through this import substitution," Dutt said. Also Read

Govt asks coal miners to triple stockpiles to avert summer blackouts

Coal India files DRHP to sell 10% stake in subsidiary SECL through IPO

Captive, commercial coal production rises 42% to 22.03 MT in October

Coal imports by imported fuel-based power plants increase marginally in Aug

Partially explored coal mines to get upfront payment waiver benefit

"Coal gasification has the potential of becoming an instrument of industrial diversification and regional development," the official said, urging coal-producing states to introduce supportive policies to attract investments in the sector. Methanol, ethanol, and ammonium nitrate used in explosives and inputs for direct reduced iron (DRI)-based steel production could be manufactured through coal gasification, he noted. Odisha and Maharashtra have already introduced incentive policies to promote coal gasification, with projects coming up in clusters in Odisha's Angul district and Maharashtra's Chandrapur belt, Dutt pointed out. He also called upon coal-rich states such as Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha to formulate policies offering incentives to investors, saying this would help attract projects and ensure that the benefits of central government schemes reach resource-rich regions. Coal gasification projects require substantial upfront capital investment as well as support at the state level in terms of electricity, water supply and taxation. Maharashtra and Odisha have taken steps in this direction, he said. Emphasising the employment potential of the sector, Dutt said gasification plants would generate jobs in downstream industries and benefit skilled and semi-skilled workers, besides strengthening local supply chains and creating additional economic activity. On coal sector reforms, Dutt said the commercial mining policy introduced in 2020 removed restrictions on end-use and sale of coal, paving the way for greater private participation. He said 137 mines had been allocated through 15 rounds of auctions, with captive and commercial mines accounting for around 20 per cent of India's total coal production. The government has also expanded the number of agencies authorised to undertake mineral exploration from 13 government agencies to 57, including 44 accredited private agencies, he informed. Dutt urged state governments to expedite land acquisition, public hearings, statutory clearances and other permissions required for operationalising coal blocks, saying delays in these processes often hinder mining projects. Faster operationalisation of auctioned coal blocks would ensure that states receive royalty and other revenue streams earlier, enabling them to fund development programmes, he stressed. Highlighting environmental initiatives, Dutt said the Coal Ministry had identified 147 mines for scientific closure over three years, of which 43 had already been scientifically closed. Scientific mine closure was not merely about technically sealing mines but also restoring degraded environments and repurposing mining areas after assessing the needs of local communities, he noted. The ministry has developed a digital tool called 'SuVikalp' to facilitate the assessment and repurposing of closed mines, he added. Dutt also stressed that the future of the coal sector should go beyond production targets and focus on productivity, technological advancement, transparency and environmental responsibility. "Mining with a conscience" should be the guiding principle for responsible miners, he said. The official also called for greater coordination between the Centre, state governments, coal companies and other stakeholders to make the sector competitive, efficient and environmentally sustainable. Union Minister for Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy, MoS for Mines Satish Chandra Dubey and Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant were present on the occasion.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: MMG, Anglo American extend $500 million nickel deal deadline
item.description: The extension comes as European regulators continue to investigate the deal and its impact on steel production.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
MMG, Anglo American extend $500 million nickel deal deadline

Marina Meireles | November 3, 2026 | 10:43 am Regulatory Issues   Top Companies   Asia   Latin America   Nickel

Niquelândia processes both nickel and manganese from Codemin and Barro Alto sites. ( Image courtesy of Anglo American. )

MMG (HKEX: 1208) and Anglo American (LON: AAL) extended the deadline for their $500-million Brazilian nickel deal by two months as European Union regulators scrutinize its potential impact on the region’s stainless steel industry.

The companies agreed to move the long-stop date from Oct. 31 to Dec. 31, 2026, rather than terminate the transaction after failing to secure regulatory approval. The extension gives t

hem time to address concerns raised by the European Commission (EC), which has launched an in-depth Phase II investigation and is expected to issue its decision by Dec. 21.

MMG said it will continue to work with the EU and Anglo American to assist the EU in its review.

Anglo agreed last year to sell its Brazilian nickel operations to MMG, prompting regulatory scrutiny over the potential impact on ferronickel supplies. The deal includes two ferronickel and two greenfield projects in Brazil.

Brazil probes Anglo’s $500M nickel sale to China’s MMG

Twists and Turns

While the deal was announced in early 2025, the EU has been reviewing its possibility and the impacts it would have on ferronickel supply for the Union’s steel production since September 2025.

The European Commission (EC) is primarily concerned about whether the acquisition could allow MMG to divert Brazilian ferronickel away from Europe. This concern arises as the EU seeks to reduce its dependence on China for ferronickel and steel production.

Those that oppose the deal say that regulators need to consider how the acquisition would impact competition between major economies in a rather unstable geopolitical environment.

Anglo American and MMG argue that there’s plenty of ferronickel availability across the market, and Chinese control wouldn’t affect competition.

Amid the EU’s review, Anglo American said it would likely close its Brazilian nickel operation if the EU blocks MMG’s acquisition, Reuters reported.

Anglo American threatens to close Brazilian nickel operation if EU blocks sale to MMG

Ahead of the original long-stop date, MMG offered guarantees to maintain ferronickel supplies to European stainless steel producers aiming to ease the EU’s concerns.

The antitrust committee decision on the deal is expected to come out by the end of 2026, leaving the companies with about 10 days to decide how to move forward.

item.title: China’s New Tunnel-Boring Export Controls Cast Shadow Over Warming Ties With India
item.description: Despite the warming ties between China and India following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, trade frictions and territorial tensions continue to simmer beneath the surface. China announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel-boring machines and other specialized …
item.dc:creator: Rudy Lu
item.content:encoded:
Despite the warming ties between China and India following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, trade frictions and territorial tensions continue to simmer beneath the surface.

China announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel-boring machines and other specialized construction equipment last week, a move Chinese analysts have interpreted as an attempt to restrict India’s strategic infrastructure development, particularly along the countries’ disputed Himalayan border.

The regulations, issued jointly by the Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs , cover tunnel-boring machines (TBMs), including shield machines and hard-rock tunnel borers, as well as critical components such as cutterheads, main drive systems and remanufacturing technologies. They also extend to specialized walking excavators capable of operating in difficult terrain and concrete-spraying machines used to reinforce tunnels at high altitudes.

The equipment is widely used in civilian infrastructure projects, such as metro systems, high-speed railways, highways, and hydropower facilities. The same machines can also be used to build military transport corridors, strategic tunnels, and other infrastructure supporting troop and equipment movements in mountainous border regions.

Set to take effect on November 18, the rules establish a two-tier export approval system.

Exporters shipping covered equipment to what Beijing describes as “sensitive countries and regions that have disputes with China” must obtain government licenses. Shipments to other destinations are subject to a simpler registration process.

Overseas organizations and individuals are prohibited from transferring or supplying Chinese-origin controlled equipment to sensitive destinations without Beijing’s approval, potentially affecting international contractors that purchase machinery in one country and redeploy it elsewhere.

Beijing has not publicly identified which countries fall under the sensitive-destination category.

The announcement has raised concerns in India, where major infrastructure projects remain dependent on imported tunneling equipment. According to a 2020 investigation by The Indian Express , industry suppliers estimated that nearly 90 percent of tunnel-boring machines deployed across India had links to China..

India’s Economic Times reported that government officials plan to consult industry stakeholders to mitigate the potential impact . While officials played down the likelihood of widespread delays to highway construction, they acknowledged that shortages of specialized machinery could affect major projects, such as the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed railway, India’s first under-construction high-speed bullet train project.

New Delhi has already begun efforts to reduce its dependence on imported equipment.

Reuters reported in August that India was preparing a $1.2 billion manufacturing incentive program aimed at attracting $1.8 billion in investment over seven years. Tunnel-boring machines are among the priority products.

Li Guangman, a senior researcher at the Kunlunce Research Institute, a leftist, pro-government Chinese think tank, said that restricting tunnel-boring equipment would allow Beijing to constrain India’s construction of military transport networks near the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border separating Indian-controlled territory from Chinese-controlled territory.

Bloomberg reported in August that India is planning to invest $4.7 billion in railway upgrades along its borders with China, Pakistan and Bangladesh over the next two years. Li argued that advanced tunneling machinery could help India build all-weather transport corridors through the Himalayas, allowing troops and military supplies to move more easily across the mountainous frontier.

The restrictions also come amid renewed territorial friction. India’s Home Ministry announced early this month standardized names for 28 locations and geographical features in Ladakh, including areas disputed with China.

China’s Foreign Ministry firmly opposed the announcement , reiterating that Beijing has never recognized the “so-called Union Territory of Ladakh,” which India had established “unilaterally and illegally.”

item.title: テンセントがオラクルからAI半導体10万個をリース、70億ドル規模－FT
item.description:
（ブルームバーグ）： 中国のテンセント・ホールディングス（騰訊）は、東南アジアでオラクルから先端のAI半導体を借り受けることで合意した。テンセントにとってAI半導体のリース契約としては過去最大規模となる。英紙フィナンシャル・タイムズ（FT）が事情に詳しい関係者の話として報じた。
報道によると、テンセントは、5年間の契約の一環として10万個の半導体を利用できるようになる。契約額は70億ドル（約1兆1000億円）に上るという。
中国のAI開発企業は米国の輸出規制を回避するため、米エヌビディア製など中国国内では入手できないAIアクセラレーターを海外で借りて利用している。中国のテクノロジー企業は、東南アジアのデータセンターの最大顧客層の一つとなっている。
テンセントとオラクルの担当者は、ブルームバーグ・ニュースのコメント要請に直ちに応じなかった。
原題：Tencent Leases AI Chips From Oracle
